title: PPL template review
summary: NH reviews the push/pull/legs template for hypertrophy. He argues that the standard order is the worst because pull and legs land back to back, prefers push in the middle, describes what each day should contain, and stresses that you are not a slave to the template. He sees PPL as lower-body focused, which suits people lacking leg development.
claims: Templates like full body or PPL dictate exercise grouping and frequency but say nothing about volume and intensity
Standard push/pull/legs is the worst order: pull (hip hinges) and legs back to back hurts one day or the other, and it is the most followed version
Running push/pull/legs twice then resting leaves pull and legs back to back at the end of the block, raising injury risk if intensity is mismanaged
Push/legs/pull is not automatically better, because for many people knee flexion loads the back more than deadlifts; deadlifts being the most taxing lift is not an objective fact
He has met more people who hurt their lower back squatting than deadlifting
Putting push in the middle (pull/push/legs or legs/push/pull) is best: it separates the two lower body days and allows extra push days
You don't need equal numbers of push, pull and leg days, and you can run PPL without rest days if intensity is managed
Pull day should open with heavy, low-rep hip hinge strength work, then rows and pull-ups, with curls supersetted
Push day should include vertical and horizontal presses, long-head triceps work (overhead extensions, skullcrushers) and rear delt flies or face pulls for shoulder health
Leg day overlaps with pull because most knee flexions involve hip hinging, which risks lower back overuse; on leg day do knee flexions, calves, and posterior chain and lower back isolation
In a PPL, legs is usually the shortest and most intense day, push the longest and least intense, and pull in between
Pull day carries the most tonnage if you deadlift
You are not a slave to the template: do chin-ups on push or calves on pull if you need them
Write your own program so you are following your own vision
PPL, with two lower days per upper day, favors leg development; upper-dominant lifters with weak legs risk overuse injuries from too much volume too fast
Natural lifters today often have dominant lower bodies, and the upper body needs a lot of volume to catch up
PPL is easy to follow, flexible in cycle length (3, 6, 12 days), and pushes you toward strength work and core movement patterns
The upper body can absorb a ton of volume
